extracted.intended_audience: student journalists and reporters learning to write court, police, and crime news
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for reporting criminal and civil court proceedings, police-court items, and crime stories: what to include, how to treat testimony, what leads and styles to use, and ethical cautions about sensationalism and prejudging cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of court news
rubrics_metrics.description: To give fair and accurate publicity to significant phases of the administration of justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The writer’s aim should be to direct the reader’s attention to those details of the proceedings (1) that are significant to him personally, (2) that affect the interests of the community, and (3) that relate to the welfare of society as a whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid playing up disgusting or scandalous phases
rubrics_metrics.description: Destructive, or anti-social, influences are found in those court stories—particularly those of criminal and divorce cases—that play up disgusting or scandalous phases of such trials in order to gratify the morbid taste of some of their readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not emphasize lurid details merely for audience titillation; avoid gratuitous sensationalism that undermines the public interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not 'try the case in the newspaper'
rubrics_metrics.description: Newspapers should not undertake to prove the innocence or the guilt of an accused person by printing whatever evidence they can secure, even though some of it would be excluded from the trial under the rules of evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid publishing evidence that would be excluded at trial or otherwise creating public opinion and arousing public feeling to such an extent as to prevent the accused person’s having the fair trial to which he is entitled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Find matters of general significance and present them clearly
rubrics_metrics.description: To find matters of general significance and interest, particularly when they are buried in legal technicalities and verbiage, and to present them clearly and attractively without sacrificing accuracy, are the main problems in handling court news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extract salient and significant phases from legal documents and proceedings; translate legal technicalities into clear copy while maintaining factual accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a matter-of-fact informative style (but make it interesting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Since much court news is of a routine character, the matter-of-fact informative news story is a frequent medium for presenting it. This does not imply that such news is necessarily dry and uninteresting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use straightforward informative style as the baseline, but bring out salient, significant phases and human-interest elements to engage casual readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop human-interest elements when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Criminal and civil cases often have a strong human interest element that, if rightly developed, may be a valuable part of the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When cases contain personal, comic, or tragic elements (especially municipal/police-court items), emphasize them responsibly to make the story appealing without sensationalizing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lead selection: determined by status of the case
rubrics_metrics.description: The lead is usually determined by the status of the case. Any one of the important points may be made the feature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the lead that best reflects the case’s current importance—verdict, sentence, motion, decision, human angle, or other pivotal fact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Body composition: summaries, excerpts, and connective material
rubrics_metrics.description: The body of court news stories usually consists of summaries of arguments, decisions, testimony, or legal documents, or of excerpts from them, with the necessary connective material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use concise summaries and selected excerpts to convey essential facts; supply connective context and background so the reader understands significance and sequence. In some instances the story may be largely a history of the case or action and of the persons involved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Testimony presentation formats
rubrics_metrics.description: Testimony in news stories is given in one of three forms: (1) the question indicated by 'Q' and the answer by 'A,' both question and answer given in one paragraph without quotation marks, (2) the question and the answer in quotation marks, each followed by the necessary explanatory matter and each in a separate paragraph, (3) a summary of the testimony of each witness in indirect quotation form, with the name of the witness at or near the beginning of the first sentence of the summarized testimony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the testimony format that best fits clarity and space constraints; ensure attribution and context so readers can assess the weight of the testimony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include the verdict and conditions under which it was rendered
rubrics_metrics.description: Among the important details: (1) the verdict and the conditions under which it was rendered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report not just the verdict but any relevant circumstances (e.g., plea bargains, hung juries, jury composition, special instructions) that affect its meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report the sentence imposed
rubrics_metrics.description: Among the important details: (2) the sentence imposed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give particulars of punishment, fines, probation, or other penalties, and note any immediate effects (e.g., remand to custody, release on bail).

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain the decision rendered and its significance
rubrics_metrics.description: Among the important details: (3) the decision rendered and its significance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Summarize the court’s ruling and explain its legal and practical implications for the parties and community.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report important testimony
rubrics_metrics.description: Among the important details: (4) important testimony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Summarize or quote key witness statements that materially affect the case, identifying source and context so readers can judge credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summarize the net results of the day's proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Among the important details: (5) net results of the day’s proceedings in a trial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a concise wrap-up of what changed that day—motions granted/denied, witness lists, developments toward resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide history of the case or action
rubrics_metrics.description: Among the important details: (6) the history of the case or action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give background chronology and prior proceedings so readers understand how the present stage was reached.

rubrics_metrics.name: State provisions of a will when reporting probate matters
rubrics_metrics.description: Among the important details: (7) provisions of a will.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report key bequests, executorships, contested clauses, and implications for heirs and estates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report liabilities, assets, and cause in bankruptcy
rubrics_metrics.description: Among the important details: (8) liabilities, assets, and cause in bankruptcy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give summary figures and principal reasons for insolvency when covering bankruptcy proceedings, focusing on items of public interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report awards or findings
rubrics_metrics.description: Among the important details: (9) the award, or finding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State the amount or remedy awarded or the factual/legal finding and its immediate consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain the grounds on which a suit is based
rubrics_metrics.description: Among the important details: (10) the grounds on which a suit is based.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe the plaintiff’s legal theory and principal factual allegations so readers can grasp the dispute’s basis.
